Case overview

Designing trust for strangers who've never met

Worckly is a two-sided marketplace concept, built solo for an independent founder around an idea rather than an existing company. The whole design problem sits on one question: what makes a stranger comfortable enough to pay another stranger for work, sight unseen.

Role
UX/UI & systems design
Solo project for an individual founder, from research through roadmap.
Structure
Two-sided marketplace
Built around a trust-tier framework rather than a feature list.
Status
Confirmed for portfolio use
Included with the founder's permission.
The brief

An idea, not yet a company

The founder came in with a concept, not a spec: a marketplace connecting people who need work done with people who can do it, without the overhead of the platforms already out there. There was no existing brand, no existing user base, and no existing trust signal to lean on.

The founder's framing was blunt: hiring a developer to build a full marketplace from scratch wasn't realistic yet, and generic job-board apps like the big incumbents treat trust as an afterthought, a badge buried in a profile page rather than something a client sees before they ever reach out. Trust had to be the differentiator from day one, not a feature added later.

The real constraint was scope, not ambition. It was one founder and one designer, no dedicated engineering team yet, so anything designed had to be buildable without a heavy custom backend in a first version. The brief settled on three trades to start (painting, plumbing, and electrical, the categories already visible in the app) rather than trying to cover every service category at launch, and on getting something demoable in weeks rather than months.

Market research

Where trust actually breaks down

The research phase focused less on competitor feature lists and more on where two-sided marketplaces lose trust: unclear pricing, no verification signal before first contact, and no recourse when a job goes badly. That shaped the trust-tier framework at the center of the whole system.

Two recurring profiles came out of that research, one from each side of the marketplace: the client trying to vet a stranger before letting them into their home, and the specialist whose actual credentials get lost in the same inbox as unlicensed competition.

Emily Clark, 36
Service Seeker · Auckland homeowner
"I just want to know this person is who they say they are before they come into my home."
About her

Emily finds most home-service help through Facebook groups and word of mouth. Every step is manual: she messages two or three people to check availability, negotiates price over text, and has no way to confirm whoever shows up is actually licensed or vetted. Once a job starts she has no visibility beyond checking in herself, and no record of what was agreed if something goes wrong.

Needs verification, visibility, and a paper trail
Sarah Smith, 41
Licensed Pro · Interior & exterior painter
"I've spent years getting certified. I need clients to see that at a glance."
About her

Sarah runs her business through referrals, a Facebook page, and word of mouth. Her licensing and insurance are real costs she carries, but nothing about how she finds work signals that investment, she's competing in the same inbox as unlicensed help. Bookings get juggled across DMs and texts, which has cost her double-bookings, and payment is negotiated informally almost every time, leaving invoices she's had to chase.

Needs visibility, credibility, and structured bookings

Both personas are composites drawn from interviews conducted during research, condensed here since the original notes weren't kept in written form. They're consistent with the demo data used throughout the actual screens (Emily Clark as the client, Sarah Smith as the specialist).

Trust-tier framework

Making trust visible before the first message

Rather than a single generic verified badge, Worckly breaks trust into three separate signals a client can check before ever messaging a specialist: a verified license confirmed against government records, a completed background check run through a verification partner, and a community rating that only kicks in once a specialist has a real track record (4.5+ across 20 or more completed jobs). Splitting it into three means a client can see exactly what's been checked, not just a vague stamp of approval.

On the specialist side, earning those badges is folded directly into onboarding rather than being a separate step: uploading a license and opting into a background check happen in the same flow as setting up a profile, so trust-building isn't an optional extra someone skips.

The badge explainer screen exists specifically so a client never has to guess what a badge means, each one names exactly what was checked and by whom.

Roadmap & stakeholder comms

Designing for a founder, not a committee

There was no roadmap template to start from, so the sequence got reasoned out from the core problem itself: a trust badge is just a design opinion until it's clear it actually changes who a client picks, so that assumption had to hold up before anything else was worth building. It got tested the way most of this project got built, in Figma, walked through informally with a handful of homeowners and tradespeople rather than a structured study.

Once that held, everything after got weighed against one question: does this need a heavy custom backend to demo. What didn't, the five-step posting wizard, specialist onboarding with license upload, and the three trust badges, became the version worth shipping first. Booking status tracking, reviews feeding the community badge, and real payment handling could all wait.

With just one founder as the stakeholder, that reasoning doubled as the relationship itself: weekly walkthroughs of the current Figma file, comments left directly on frames instead of a separate ticketing tool, and priority decided together in those calls rather than handed down from a plan.

Interface

Screens

Three flows carry the client side of the marketplace: posting a job, tracking it once a specialist is booked, and closing the loop with a review once it's done.

Posting a job

Posting a job is a five-step wizard rather than a single long form: pick an industry, describe the work, confirm the service address, review everything together, then get a booking confirmation with a live status tracker. Splitting it up keeps each screen focused on one decision at a time instead of asking for everything at once.

Reviewing before confirming

Before anything is booked, a Project Summary screen pulls the job details, payment information, and any additional notes into one place for a final check, the same review-before-you-commit pattern used throughout the rest of the flow.

Tracking, completing, and reviewing a job

Once booked, the same project detail view carries through the Pending tab, showing the assigned specialist, a step tracker for the job's progress, and payment status. After a job wraps up, a short review prompt captures a star rating and quick-tap tags for what went well, and completed jobs stay on record with the final cost, so a client's job history doubles as a receipt archive.
